turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Wednesday, the second of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go. [excited] Claire, what's on top?
Three things. The truce over the Strait of Hormuz breaks a second time in a week — and this time the strikes land inside Iran.
The one everyone in tech is arguing about — Nvidia is reported to be buying Hugging Face, the place every rival's chips download their models from.
And the closer: Thailand's economy is stalling, and a whole generation is buying luck by the amulet. [wry] The gods, it turns out, have a media plan.
[chuckles] Okay, I need that last one. But start me on the strait.
So. A week ago, American forces hit an island in the strait. On the first of September, they went further — strikes on the Iranian mainland, at Bandar Abbas and Chabahar on the southern coast.
Mainland. That's the escalation.
That's the escalation. Central Command says it answered fresh attempts by the Revolutionary Guard to hit shipping in the strait and to target American troops.
And Tehran? [curious]
Tehran called its reply a — quote — decisive operation, and said US bases and interests across the region were now being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones.
[thoughtful] That sounds like a war, not a skirmish.
It depends who's narrating. Washington frames it as a response, narrow by design — a stalemate over the chokepoint, with neither side willing to cede control.
And Beijing?
Beijing says economic warfare and maximum pressure won't resolve anything, and wants free navigation restored immediately. Its oil rides through that strait, remember.
Right. And the view from Doha?
Al Jazeera reads it as an escalating two-way war with no off-ramp — a fresh oil-and-inflation shock the whole region will wear.
Four capitals, four stories. [thoughtful] What did the market do?
Brent crude settled above ninety-one US dollars — firmest in weeks. A fifth of the world's seaborne oil moves through that strait.
So here's my naive question. Do the strikes actually reopen it?
[deadpan] That is exactly the question. And the honest answer from the sceptics is no. The Cato Institute calls the campaign a fool's errand that risks a forever war.
Meaning air strikes can punish, but they can't force the lane open.
Exactly. Experts at The Hill warn the strikes may not break Tehran, which sees this as a war of survival — and that Washington is trapped in a cycle without defining what victory even looks like.
[sighs] Hold that thought, because it walks straight into the money desk.

One more thread first. The other oil story of the week — Venezuela. Caracas has finally put numbers to the deal it signed with Washington: twenty-five years, sixty-five billion barrels, and just nineteen US dollars a barrel flowing to Venezuela.
[gasps] Nineteen dollars, against a benchmark of what?

Sixty-five. The spread is Washington's read on who won. And it pulls a major supplier toward the United States, which is precisely why Beijing feels squeezed from both ends — the strait and the contract.
It does. Because the same oil jump lands inside an inflation scare. Name the regime and everything follows: this is hawkish repricing meeting a supply shock.
Hawkish — that's the new Fed chair.
Kevin Warsh. At Jackson Hole on the twenty-ninth of August, he said plainly that inflation is not beaten. A month ago the market priced the September meeting as a near-certain cut.
And now?
Now it's a coin-toss between a hold and a hike. The meeting is the fifteenth and sixteenth of September, and the jobs report lands around the fifth.
Okay, give me the levels — spelled out, for the people doing dishes.
[amused] For the dishwashers. Gold fell toward four thousand three hundred fifty US dollars, about eight per cent below its January record. Bitcoin stayed heavy near seventy-eight thousand.
And the dollar?
The dollar firmed, near ninety-nine point six on the index. The ten-year Treasury yield backed up to about four point seven seven per cent — which means bond prices fell.
So what's the one thing to notice?
The broken pairing. Gold and bitcoin — the two debasement trades — fell together while the dollar rose. That shape is a rates story overpowering a fear story.
[curious] Say more. Normally a war bids gold up.
Normally, yes. When the anti-fiat assets sell off into a geopolitical shock, the market is telling you higher-for-longer, not risk-off, is driving. This is explanation, by the way, not advice.
Always. And a forecast is a forecast.
A coin-toss is not a forecast. The trackers disagree, and where a print is awaited — the jobs number, the meeting — we hold it, we don't guess it.
So in one breath — what does it mean for the four things you track?

A firmer dollar and stubborn real yields are the headwind on gold and bitcoin — the week's casualties. Global bonds stay pinned. And world equities held near their highs, which is the vulnerability, not the comfort.
[curious] Why the vulnerability?
Because the loop is forming — a strait keeps oil high, oil keeps the Fed hawkish, and eventually a hawkish Fed tests the one thing still standing near its record.
Good. Now bring it home to Singapore.
Two moves. First, from the fifteenth of September, a licensed moneylender's unsecured loan comes with a three-business-day cooling-off window. Cancel inside it and you owe no interest.
[amused] A pause button on a decision people make under pressure.
Exactly that. Though the sceptic's note matters — it only touches licensed lenders. The real harm, the loan sharks, sits outside it.
And the second move?

The feed. Building on the age-thirteen line, the government signalled harder teenager safeguards — autoplay off by default, daily time limits under study, and a warning that platforms that won't comply could be forced to raise their minimum age from thirteen to eighteen.
Legislation when?
Targeted for early twenty twenty-seven. And the trade backdrop is hot — non-oil exports rose more than twenty-four per cent on the year in July.
Let's do silicon. The Nvidia story — walk carefully.

Carefully is right. The Information reports Nvidia has struck a deal to buy Hugging Face for around thirteen billion US dollars. Reported — not announced. No signed contract, no filing, both firms declined to comment.
So why does it matter, if it's just a rumour with a big number?
Because of what Hugging Face is. It's the neutral warehouse — the place a developer on an AMD or Intel chip downloads the same open model as one on an Nvidia card.
[skeptical] And a chip company would own the warehouse everyone shares.

That's the objection, and it writes — sorry — it's obvious the moment you say it. Can a referee own a team? Nvidia doesn't open-source its own software. The fear is it steers the whole ecosystem its way.

And there's a second silicon story riding alongside it. OpenAI published benchmarks for its own in-house chip — codename Jalapeño — claiming it does up to nearly twice the work per kilowatt of Nvidia's top part.
[skeptical] Claiming. Who checked?
Analysts were in the room — but only for selected runs, not the full suite. So better than last week's numbers, still not independent. A vendor's own scorecard, witnessed in part.
Is there a home-lab angle?
A lovely one. The biggest open model released this week, from Tencent, needs about nine hundred gigabytes just to hold its weights. That's a full data-centre node.
[laughs] So I can download it, I just can't run it.
You can admire it. The model you actually run at home is a smaller one, about twenty-four gigabytes on a single card. And you download both from — you guessed it — the hub that's changing hands.
Who owns the shelf. [thoughtful] Okay, quick gear hit. The Kit?
A pair of display glasses from Even Realities — five hundred ninety-nine US dollars. A monochrome heads-up display in a thirty-five-gram frame, and here's the twist: no camera, no speakers at all.
Privacy as an omission. I kind of love that.
Two-day battery, which is the number that separates it from the pack. Sold as a productivity tool, not a gadget.
And the buy-it-once desk — the Atelier?
Everyday backpacks, judged from the zipper out. The single clearest tell of quality is a YKK zipper versus a no-name coil that fails first and can't be replaced.
Give me the money line.

A two-hundred-fifty-dollar Evergoods or Peak Design pack is about ninety per cent of a five-hundred-dollar one for daily use. And a Prada nylon backpack at twenty-five hundred is the same fibre family as a sixty-dollar pack.
[scoffs] A ten-to-twenty-times markup for a triangle.
Your words. [wry] But yes. And the buy-once case is the warranty — GORUCK, Peak Design, Osprey will repair or replace a pack for life, no receipt.
For the tropics, though — leather and waxed canvas?
Skip them as daily drivers. In this humidity they trap damp and grow mould in a closet. Favour the laminated synthetics that shrug off a four-o'clock squall and dry by evening.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[excited] Astrophotography, Claire. And here's the hook that got me — the camera sees what your eye physically cannot.
Explain that.
You don't take one photo. You take dozens, or hundreds, of exposures — they call them subs — throw away the bad ones, and stack the rest to pull a coloured nebula out of a sky that looks pure black.
Computational photography, basically.

Basically. And the thing that blew the doors open is the smart telescope. You point an app at a target and the box finds it, tracks it, stacks it. The new Seestar S-fifty Pro landed a week ago — nine hundred ninety-nine US dollars.
[curious] And that works from a balcony in Singapore?

This is the beautiful part. Singapore's sky is Bortle eight — so bright the Milky Way is invisible to the naked eye. But nebulae glow in narrow wavelengths, so a narrowband filter lets you image them anyway. From an HDB balcony.
And if you go past the one-tap box?
[curious] Then you're into the real rig, and the community mantra is spend on the mount first — the thing that holds a star to a single pixel over minutes. The glass comes second.
And the other half is software, right?

Half the craft. The professional suite, PixInsight, has a famous learning curve and a cult to match — but a free tool called Siril now does most of it, and the new AI sharpening tools run right inside it.
What's the catch? There's always a catch.
[laughs] The community will tell you themselves. It's a money pit with a next tier always visible. It's mostly not doing astrophotography — the running joke is one clear night a month.
And the purists fighting the one-tap crowd.
Constantly. Plus the AI-processing worry — the tools are so good people ask whether they're enhancing your data or hallucinating detail that was never there.
[thoughtful] Which is the whole issue in miniature, isn't it. A prettier picture that drifts from the thing that made it.
[warmly] Look at you, threading the theme.
Speaking of pretty pictures with thin evidence — Screen and Sound. Erykah Badu is back, sixteen years after her last proper album, in a full collaboration with the producer The Alchemist.
The reviews?
Warm — Rolling Stone calls it her best since two thousand eight. But here's the caveat: the aggregate score of eighty-five rests on a single logged review.
[skeptical] One review is not an aggregate.
It is not. Very promising, unproven — give it a fortnight before anyone says classic.
The Good Life — quick one.
Grand Seiko made a stunning peach-pink watch dial. Seven thousand six hundred US dollars — and thirty pieces, sold at a single boutique in Atlanta.
So effectively un-buyable from here.
Scarcity priced as craft. The dial is real; the exclusivity is a marketing decision.
Family desk — this one matters to a lot of our listeners.

A large study — over a hundred thousand records — finds the wellbeing dip when a child moves up to secondary school is real, common, and usually passes. It tracks the school move itself, not just growing up.
[warmly] So a struggling Secondary One kid is often just a kid adjusting.

Often, yes. The biggest drop is in motivation, not mood — so watch engagement, not just grades. Three moves: guard sleep, keep one steady friendship or activity, and watch whether they still care. General guidance, not medical advice.
And the body — Fitness.
A thirty-year study of nearly a hundred and fifty thousand adults puts the strength-training sweet spot at ninety to a hundred and twenty minutes a week — and finds no extra benefit past two hours.
[warmly] So the ceiling is a permission slip. I can stop feeling guilty.
Pair it with cardio and the death-risk number roughly halves. Also not medical advice — and the percentages are directional, not gospel.
And one to book?
Coldplay is in Tokyo this week. The Singapore Grand Prix adds its first-ever Sprint in October. And a new Korean spot cures its own pork in what it calls the city's first Himalayan salt room.

Coldplay is in Tokyo this week — days away — with a Seoul pair the weekend after. The Grand Prix adds its first-ever Sprint over the ninth to eleventh of October. And a Fukuoka sumo basho in November for the reader who plans the trip, not just the ticket.
[warmly] And the soft yen makes the whole thing cheaper than it's been in years.
Near a hundred and sixty to the dollar. The currency, not the calendar, is the argument for going now.
[laughs] A salt room. Of course.
Which brings us, finally, to the long read. [pause] Slow down with me for this one.
[thoughtful] Thailand.
Thailand is posting its weakest growth in about thirty years. And its under-thirties are pouring money and screen-time into amulets, fortune-tellers, lucky colours. They call it mutelu.
How big, really?
Eighty-eight per cent of Thai consumers say they believe in it. Researchers found that nearly half turn to it specifically after investment losses or hardship.
[drawn out] So it's a hedge. An informal one, for people locked out of the returns their parents had.
That's the argument. Superstition as a barometer of anxiety — it boomed in the two thousand six coup, again in the twenty sixteen slump, and now.
Give me one image from it.

A boy-spirit shrine they call Egg Boy — people petition it for lottery numbers, and when a wish lands they repay it with toys, firecrackers and fizzy drinks. And it's all on TikTok — live fortune-tellers reading cards to thousands at once.
[amused] Luck as a content genre.
Marketers even coined a word for baking it into product launches. Devotion, rendered as a feed.
And you said the state is in on it.

The tourism authority has made spiritual travel a formal pillar of its twenty twenty-six plan. Belief is being industrialised — because, honestly, it may be one of the few high-margin things a stalling middle-income economy can still make and sell.
[curious] And there's a darker edge?
There is. Chinese buyers are now the marginal customers, and with them came grey capital — an immigration bureau warned in July that the amulet trade risks becoming a money-laundering channel.
[exhales] A stalling economy's young hedging their future, and a state learning to sell them the hedge.
That's the line. When the Financial Times writes it up in three weeks — remember which desk had it first.
[warmly] What a book.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
